en: Compiled by the Chan Master Xiuhu of the Brahmā Heaven Fire-Net Nine Planets School. The twenty-eight lunar mansions revolve to the left in the heavens;
by calculating them, one may know the positions where people commit transgressions. From the first year of the Wude era of the Great Tang, the year Wuyin (618 CE), until the Xian... [text continues]
Including the fifteenth year, Jia-wu,
a total of two hundred and fifty-seven years have elapsed.
The diagrams of the nine celestial bodies according to the Brahma-fire system, as well as those of the two stars, An and Xu, are contained herein.
"However, regarding the locations of all the stars,
if one observes them with certainty,
the good and ill fortune of a lifetime will not fail by even a single instance; it is the ultimate in divine mystery," and so forth.
First, regarding the deity of the eclipse, Rāhu:

Oṃ rāhūnāsurarājāya se maśatruya nāmavidhe svasti kuru svāhā. As for the oral instruction on making offerings to the planet Rāhu with coins: offer them toward the direction of Chou (Northwest) and Yin (Northeast).
The ages of nineteen, twenty-eight, thirty-seven, forty-six, fifty-five, sixty-four, seventy-three, eighty-two, and ninety-one are all greatly inauspicious.
If one reaches this year and stays [under its influence], it is ominous.
The star is hidden and invisible;
it is also named Rāhu.
One is named Rāśi, one is named Pītapatākā,
and one is named Agnirajas.
When one's personal destiny is approached,
there is anxiety regarding loss of office and position,
and one is beset by grave illness.
There will be the dispersal of wealth and property, mourning due to bereavement, and verbal disputes.
If a king fails to sacrifice to the deities, these calamities will arise; by cultivating merit beforehand, one may ward them off.

It is said that for great auspiciousness, one should offer "Yuan-shen" (Original Spirit) money and painted images of the offended deities as offerings. Furthermore, human life belongs to the Great Clear Heaven (Dàqīngtiān).
In this year, all matters will proceed as desired;
whatever you seek shall surely be attained.
Whether traveling or engaging in daily affairs, everything will bring great good fortune.
The King of Constellations, the Earth-Abiding One (Bhauma), resides in the center of the two [spheres] during the four seasons;
his mantra is: *Namo oṃ jayāyai svāhā*. Furthermore, another mantra is said: [Namo oṃ jayāyai svāhā].
Oṃ śāntikāraka svastaye puṣṭike svāhā. Furthermore, there is this mantra.

Oṃ śu śukarāgra-dvāra-vāra-vāra-ja-nāmā-sthāne śrī svāhā. [Offer this] during the spring at the southeast (Sūn), summer at the southwest (Kun), autumn at the northwest (Gan), and winter at the northeast (Gen). For the intercalary month of midsummer, offer a single plate of fruit as a sacrifice. The oral instructions state that the direction is not fixed.
In the spring, one should know the remaining [years] in sequence starting from the southeast (Xun).
The years twenty-one, twenty-nine, thirty-eight, forty-seven, fifty-six, sixty-five, seventy-four, eighty-three, and ninety-two are all extremely inauspicious.
When one's age reaches this lunar mansion, it is the Saturn of the Central Palace.
This star has a circumference of ninety *li* and belongs to the domain of the state of Chu.
This mansion is the most inauspicious.
When this mansion (Nakṣatra) presides over the palace or obstructs a person, one must be upright and cautious regarding illness and imprisonment.
For the nobleman, it is a year of grave misfortune; it is called the Year of the Earth Planet (Ti-xing).
One should not dare to offend it.
Its form is like that of a Brahmin;
it has a cow-horn crown upon its head and holds a mendicant’s staff (khakkhara) in its hand.
One should offer a platter of seasonal summer fruits as a sacrifice to this king who brings calamity.
One should send offerings of money for the life-destiny spirit and the primordial soul,
paint the forms of the deities offended, and offer them worship; then,
drive them away with yellow garments.
One must certainly eliminate calamities and increase blessings and longevity for one’s natal year.
Under the constellation of Chixu (Jupiter), all matters may not go as desired;
for men, it is unfavorable for official advancement, and for women, unfavorable for their husbands.
Avoid the third and ninth months, as well as days of the *geng* and *xin* stems.
It is said that the North Star (*Beichenxing*) and the Water Star (*Shuixing*), the king of stars, preside over the three months of winter.
The mantra is: *Oṃ kusidatadhitadhitirāya ya ya ji ji niti svāhā*. It is further stated: [as above].
Oṃ mudan kṣasvamināmanīkrama svāhā. Furthermore, the heart-mantra is as follows:

Oṃ susthira svāhā. Using oil for an offering toward the north during the months of midsummer, one will receive [the following years]: thirty-two, twenty-one, thirty-three, nineteen, forty-eight, fifty-seven, sixty-six, seventy-five, eighty-four, ninety-three; these are slightly auspicious.
When one reaches this year, the asterism is named Beichen (North Star).
It is also called Chansing (Leaping Star) and Dixin (Dripping Star).
It spans one hundred li in circumference and belongs to the fiefdoms of Yan and Zhao.
If it falls upon one's natal year,
it presides over sorrow and verbal disputes, as well as being summoned by thieves and bandits.
The appearance of this deity is that of a woman.
The leader wears a monkey crown and holds paper and brush in his hands.
In the month of midsummer, the king shall perform an oil sacrifice;
it is appropriate to offer a rite to the Big Dipper to ward off calamity.
Count these twelve lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*).
Starting from the mansion immediately below the birth month, count one day for each mansion moving to the left until you reach the mansion of the birth date; thus it is known, and so forth.
If one has already set out on this journey, it will not differ from the fate of the original person; their life shall belong to the Youxian Heaven, and none of their undertakings will succeed.
For a man, it is unfavorable for official service; for a woman, it is unfavorable for her husband.
One must avoid the day of Bingxu in the fourth lunar month.
The fourth is the Great White Star in the west, which is Venus, the deity of gold. Its king presides over the three months of autumn and is radiant by day.
The homage is: *Oṃ vevi viśva svāhā*. Furthermore, there is another mantra: [omitted].
Oṃ śuklarāgadoṣa-vāraṇa-nāma-sthiti-śrī svāhā. One should always perform this sacrifice with raw coins during the middle month of autumn, facing [the deity].

In the west, the years for making offerings are forty-three, twenty-two, thirty-one, forty-four, forty-nine, fifty-eight, sixty-seven, seventy-six, eighty-five, and ninety-four; these are slightly inauspicious.
When one reaches the year Na-xie,
this is the planet Venus, the quintessence of metal from the west.
This star is also known as Dabai (Great White).
One is named Changgeng and the other is named Naxie;
these stars span one hundred li in circumference and belong to the astrological domain of the state of Qin.
If one encounters their own year of birth,
there may be weeping, wailing, and the calamities of war;
the form [of the deity] is like that of a woman.
Wearing a crown upon his head and dressed in white silk garments,
he plucks at stringed instruments and brings calamity to others.
The King should regularly use uncoined money to offer sacrifice to it during the month of mid-autumn.
When one’s year of birth reaches this star,
one should wear white robes and perform a *zhao* ritual to thank the primal spirit of one's destiny (*benming yuanshen*), thereby cultivating fields of merit.
This is most auspicious.
Human life is subject to the Flying Hammer Heaven; all matters are favorable, and anxieties and afflictions are resolved.
For men, wealth and official rank are appropriate; wives and children shall remain in harmony.
One’s livelihood will increase ten-thousandfold.
The mantra of the Five Great Sun Secrets, the Sun and Stars, is as follows:
*Namo ratnatrayāya, namo suriyasavarnakīratnarājāya, oṃ amoghasiddhi svāhā*. On the winter solstice day, one should perform an offering with various precious gems.

For those facing the directions of Mao and Chen, the years of great good fortune are fifty-four, twenty-three, thirty-two, forty-one, fifty-five, nineteen, sixty-eight, seventy-seven, eighty-six, and ninety-five.
When one reaches this lunar station in their years,
it presides over the Great Yang and belongs to the Sun;
its star revolves for a circumference of fifteen hundred li.
One day completes one circuit of the heavens.
If it coincides with one's natal year,
there will be the promotion of rank, advancement of emolument, and joyful events.
One will always receive the guidance and support of noble persons, and all undertakings will proceed with success.
On the winter solstice, if a king performs a sacrifice using various precious gems, it will bring great auspiciousness. The mantra of this star is inconceivable.
If one wears [this talisman] with a sincere heart and makes offerings for one year,
one will not die an untimely death, and so forth.
One’s life shall be protected by the pervasive light, and all matters will accord with one's wishes.
The celestial deities will protect one another, so that no real difficulties shall arise;
whatever one pursues will be opened up and facilitated, and blessings and prosperity will arrive of their own accord.
Sixth, regarding the Fire of the South, the planet Venus (Śukra), the Fire King who presides over the three months of summer: the mantra of the Fire Star is as follows.
I take refuge in Oṃ Mahālikā Svāhā. Furthermore, the mantra is:
Oṃ Agarakarūṇye Nāma Svāhā. One should perform the fire sacrifice during the middle month of summer.
Offer it facing south.
The years sixty-five, twenty-four, thirty-three, forty-two, fifty-one, sixty-six, nineteen, seventy-eight, eighty-seven, and ninety-six are all inauspicious years.
When the year reaches this star—
also known as the Southern Planet of Mars (Māṅgalya),
and also known as the Four-Benefits Star (Caturmukha)— it is so designated.
The first is named Xuhan;
its star is seventy li in circumference and belongs to the division of the state of Wei.
If one encounters the end of another's life,
there will inevitably arise disputes and verbal strife,
and they shall be entangled by illness.
The deity’s form is like that of a non-Buddhist (tīrthika);
he wears a donkey-horned crown upon his head,
and his four hands hold weapons, including a sword-blade.
In the month of midsummer, the king performs the fire sacrifice;
those whose years have reached this point [participate].
When a gentleman encounters good fortune,
his official duties advance and increase; when a petty person encounters good fortune, [his conduct likewise advances].
Calamities do not arise;
by honoring [this], one is free from misfortune and retribution.
Human life belongs to the clouds and the sky.
The celestial deities protect one another;
they dare not harbor calamity.
Wealth and resources are full and overflowing.
Blessings and prosperity will extend far and wide;
though there may be slight sorrow,
it shall resolve itself of its own accord, leaving no suffering.
The seventh, the planet Ketu, the devourer:
The mantra is *Oṃ vajra-ketu-nānākṣatrarāja hūṃ*. One should draw this form and perform offerings in a deep chamber to appease it.
Turning misfortune into fortune,
he had not yet presented his offerings;
Rāhu was wearing a jewel-encrusted ornament.
The Sun, Moon, Ji, and Dui all wear garments of brocade and embroidery.
The years seventy-six, twenty-five, thirty-four, forty-three, fifty-two, sixty-one, seventy-nine, eighty-eight, and ninety-seven are all inauspicious.
When the year reaches this point, Ketu is likewise a hidden star;
it is also called Pucchā and Mahāgūḍha.
The head was hidden and could not be seen;
though he moved about, his form was indeterminate.
When he approached a person, [he would appear].
Officials are most often subjected to overcrowding;
those who seek office do not succeed,
and their duties are frequently transferred.
Bound by official documents and entangled in legal affairs;
much anxiety and illness.
This star is inauspicious.
The king does not perform sacrifices;
when the year reaches this point, one must present offerings to the Lord of Fate of the Five Paths.
One should paint the form of this deity.
One should perform offerings in a secluded chamber to avert [calamities].
Transform misfortune into fortune;
for human life is subject to the deity Uṣṇīṣa.
Whatever one undertakes will not go as intended;
one's actions will bring no benefit;
husband and wife will weep.
Alternatively, when shedding tears,
one should avoid the fifth and sixth lunar months, the days of the *jia* and *yi* stems, and the eighth day of the month,
which is called the "Great Yin Month" (*dàyīn yuè*) when the sky is clear.
Oṃ caṇḍāla-akṣa-tarājāya nāma-sthiti svāhā. One should always perform this on the day of the summer solstice.
Various precious gems and water offerings should be presented facing the directions of the猴 (Shen) and 雞 (You) [the seventh and eighth lunar months] during the following years:
eighty-seven, twenty-six, thirty-five, forty-five, fifty-three, sixty-two, seventy-one, eighty-eight, eighty-nine, and ninety-eight.
When one's years reach this stellar position,
it is the Great Yin;
it belongs to the Moon.
Its circumference is one thousand five hundred li.
It completes one circuit around the world in a single day.
It is most auspicious for those whose birth-year destiny it encounters.
One's official rank will increase and one's emoluments will advance; all undertakings will proceed with success.
One will receive the patronage and guidance of noble persons and shall constantly experience matters of joy and celebration.
On the day of the summer solstice,
the king performed a water sacrifice using various precious gems and jade;
it was at this point that the year’s cycle reached its current stage.
In matters of affairs, harmony prevails; in seeking office, one’s endeavors will succeed, and all undertakings are most auspicious.
However, if a person’s life-force belongs to the Wei (微) star, they will face a thousand or ten hundred misfortunes regarding the gods.
They shall encounter illness with fear of death, suffer crop failures in fields and silkworms, and have cause for anxiety over matters involving government officials.
Avoid the first and ninth months, as well as days of the *bing* and *ding* stems.
In the east, the King of the Age Star (*Sāgara*) presides over the three months of spring;
when Jupiter is bright, one should recite: *Namo samantabuddhānām oṃ indrāya svāhā*. Furthermore, there is another mantra: [insert mantra].
Oṃ bharasapatti namadhipitavānyanāmamala bodhaye svāhā. One should always perform this offering with various jewels during the middle month of spring.
Offer [the items] facing east.
The years ninety-eight, twenty-seven, thirty-six, forty-five, fifty-four, sixty-three, seventy-two, eighty-one, ninety-nine, and nineteen are all times of great auspiciousness.
The planet that reaches the position of Ullambusa is Jupiter (Venus).
It is the essence of wood from the east;
it is also named Chaitra.
This star revolves within a circumference of one hundred li and belongs to the divisions of Lu and Wei.
When it aligns with a person's natal destiny,
it brings the advancement of office and the increase of emolument.
May all things be auspicious.
His divine form is like that of a high minister;
he wears a green robe.
He wears the *hai* cap and holds flowers and fruit in his hands.
The king always [performs this rite] during the second month of spring.
One should worship with various precious jewels.
When the year reaches this lunar station, it is auspicious to engage in social intercourse with persons of noble rank, and marriages will be harmonious.
This year is a time of great good fortune.
One’s life is protected by the High Storehouse Heaven (Takakura-ten), and all matters will be harmonized.
Whatever one pursues will accord with one's wishes, and there will be benefit in all comings and goings.
One shall dwell in peace, and one’s descendants will flourish and prosper.

The Mantra of the Seven Luminous Stars of the Northern Dipper: *Namaḥ samantānāraṇāra-pracaṭa hūṃ*. The Mantra of the Nine Planets: *Namo oṃ grahebhyaḥ svāhā*. Regarding the deities of the eclipses (*graha-devatās*):

from the first month until the end of the year, they constantly reside in two constellations—*Śraviṣṭhā* (Wing) and *Jyeṣṭhā* (Tension). Regarding the deities of the tails: from the first month until the end of the year, they occupy these two constellations—*Mūlā* (Tail) and *Pūrva-āṣāḍhā* (Lower Head)—without exception. This is according to the original text; as stated in this sutra: [The text continues with the specific planetary influences and the corresponding mantras. **Note:** The provided source text contains transliterated Sanskrit mantras and technical astrological terminology related to the *nakṣatras* (lunar mansions) and *grahas* (planetary deities). The translation reflects the liturgical and ritual context of the passage. The mantras are presented as they appear in the source, followed by the explanation of the planetary movements through the constellations. The final section refers to the authority of the scripture (*sūtra*) for these astrological correlations.
Ordinary people know only of the seven luminaries; they do not realize there are two empty stars called Rāhu and Ketu.
These stars remain in hidden positions and are invisible, yet when they encounter the sun or the moon, an eclipse occurs.
He is called the Eclipse Deity (Rāhu).
Ketu is the tail of the Eclipse Deity;
he is called the Leopard’s Tail (Bhṛṅgīśa).
If one's annual cycle reaches this lunar mansion,
one must by all means draw the image of the offended deity,
make offerings in a secluded room, and burn paper money to expel its influence.
Thus, calamities will not arise.
If one encounters malevolent stars, they must be warded off;
none of these [stars] will oppose or violate what has been committed.
Thus, misfortune is immediately transformed into good fortune; conversely, if one does not believe, good fortune is immediately transformed into misfortune.
When encountering auspicious stars, there will be layers upon layers of celebration, and one’s merit and virtue will be sovereign and free.
When encountering calamities caused by malevolent stars,
officials and nobles who fall victim to them shall be demoted or stripped of their rank;
however, one should simply face the Big Dipper during the hour of Hai (9–11 p.m.).
Worship your natal star with a sincere heart.
By no means should you urinate facing north, as this will shorten your lifespan.
You should contemplate the truth and cultivate goodness; thus you shall obtain blessings and wealth.
If these are not removed, disasters will arise in competition.
The Method of Paying Homage to the Northern Dipper by Ge Xian Gong for Subduing the Supreme Mysterious Ninefold North Pole of the Northern Dipper.
From princes and nobles down to the commoners and the people,
all without exception belong to the Seven Stars of the Northern Dipper;
one must always treat them with reverence and respect.
One shall not encounter untimely calamities or malevolent events.
One shall universally rescue all people from their distress,
attain longevity and increased years, and be free from all disasters and misfortunes.
Furthermore, by making offerings with a sincere heart to one’s own natal spirit and original soul,
one shall fully attain the fulfillment of human destiny and fortune;
all calamities, misfortunes, and obstructions shall be cleared away.
All this arises from failing to show reverence toward the stellar constellations and being unaware that one has offended them;
thus, as one proceeds in obscurity, calamities naturally arrive.
To ward it off brings great good fortune.
On the days of worshipping one's natal *benming* (original destiny) spirit and *yuanshen* (original soul), there are six such days in a year.
Simply, on the day of one’s own birth, with a sincere heart,
cut auspicious money (suínián qián) from high-quality paper according to one's age;
prepare tea and fruit offerings in three layers and spread out a clean bed.
Incense was burned, and with a devout heart he faced the Big Dipper.
Having prostrated himself twice, he addressed it, saying:
"Living in seclusion with few companions, I have long sought spiritual efficacy through the Way and have constantly beheld your venerable form."
On this day of my natal year, I reverently offer silver coins and celestial fruits as an offering to the Star of the Northern Dipper and to the spirit-form of my natal deity.
May this ensure longevity throughout my life and that I be free from all calamities.
The spirit and soul find peace;
the primal spirit attains autonomy.
When I was young, I was driven by worldly affairs toward distant lands.
Perform two prostrations, burn paper money, and join the palms in offering.
┌○ The Planet Pòjūn (Prajāpati) holds the Great Position for those born in the hour of Wǔ.
└○ The Planet Liánzhēng (Rudra) does not perform the ablution for those born in the hours of Zǐ, Chén, or Shēn.
└○ Wénqū Star: Wēihuì; for those born in the years Zǐ, Mǎo, or Yǒu.
├○ Lùcún Star: Lùhuì; for those born in the years Yín or Xū.
┌─┴○ Jùmén Star: Zhēnwén; for those born in the years Hài or Chōu.
Regarding those born under the Xi Zizi (希子子) branch governed by the star Tanlang (貪狼):
as stated in various texts on fortune and destiny (*lùmìngshū*),
such persons belong to the category of those governed by the star Pòjūn (破軍).
One who consumes one *sheng* [of grain] per day will live for eighty years. Those born in the Year of the Horse or Sheep, male or female, are styled Dajingzi and belong to the Wugu Star people;
they consume over one *shi* [of grain] per day and will live for eighty-five years. Those born in the Year of the Snake or Sheep, male or female, are styled Dadongzi.

One born under the star Lianzhen (廉貞) will eat slightly more than one *sheng* of grain per day and live to eighty years of age. Those born in the years of the Dragon (*chén*) or Monkey (*shēn*), whether male or female, have a name artistry that does not neighbor the *zǐ* branch.
One belongs to the Wenqu (文曲) star person.

Daily consumption: four *sheng* and more; lifespan: ninety years. For those born in the Year of the Hare (*mǎo*) or the Year of the Rooster (*yǒu*), the male and female names are "Wei-hui" (Subtle Wisdom) and "Zi" (Child).
They belong to the constellation of Luksun (Luk-sun-xing).

Daily consumption: five *sheng* and more; lifespan: eighty years. For those born in the Year of the Tiger (*yín*) or the Year of the Dog (*shù*), the male and female names are "Lukcun-hui" (Assembly of Luksun) and "Zi" (Child).
One born under the Ju-men (Great Gate) star will consume eight sheng or more of grain daily and live for eighty years. Those born in the Chou or Hai year, whether male or female,
have the name Zhen-wenzi and belong to the Tan-lang (Greed Wolf) star.
Daily consumption: two *sheng* and some remainder. Life span: sixty-five years. For those born in the year of the Rat, the names for sons and daughters are Si-xi and Shen-zi.

All Tathāgatas have spoken this Auspicious Mantra for Shattering All Obstructions Caused by Planets and Constellations: *Oṃ sarvanakṣatrasamaye śrīye śāntika kuru svāhā*. Whether it be a male *jiti* (celestial net) or a female *diti* (earthly net), if one wishes to know misfortunes and calamities, they depend solely on what is transgressed in the year of one's destiny; there is nothing that will not be known. As for a person whose year of destiny has little auspiciousness and much inauspiciousness, while it may be possible to know this and avoid it, one must not sit idly by and accept such disasters. Thus it is said: "If you do not act... [text fragment].
The Brahmā Fire Mandala. One fascicle of the Brahmā Fire Mandala, respectfully addressed to Mahābrahmā Deva-rāja, Śakra Devendra-rāja, Yama T'ien-tzŭ, and the Great Deities of the Five Paths.
The Lord of Mount Tai, the Lord of Destiny, and the Lord of Fortune;
the deities of the twelve palaces, the seven luminaries, and the nine executors;
the twenty-eight lunar mansions, yakṣas, and yakṣiṇīs.
The Vaiśvānaras, Vaiśvadevas, Bhūtas, Devas, and other such distinguished,
protective, and virtuous deities who are to be invoked for protection;
as well as the various great and small deities who guard the household and the dwelling.
Together with the unspeakably unspeakable numbers of lands and the various classes of beings born through the six realms and four modes of birth within the trichiliocosm, may [Name],
on this auspicious day and favorable hour of this month, [make such-and-such a vow].
He prepared divine offerings and an unobstructed array of requisites;
thus, the great aspiration of this noble being may be known, and so forth.
Next, the invitation: facing the east, join the palms. This concludes the above.
The following is a record of the notes written on the margins of the paper, which I now transcribe here:

1. Rāhu is greatly malevolent; 2. Earth is slightly malevolent; 3. Water is auspicious; 4. Metal is moderately auspicious; 5. Fire is greatly auspicious; 6. Wood is slightly malevolent; 7. Mercury (Budha) is greatly auspicious; 8. Jupiter (Bṛhaspati) is moderately auspicious; 9. Venus (Śukra) is greatly auspicious.
This is called the "Mantra Method of All Minor Devas": extend the middle finger of the right hand while forming a fist with the remaining fingers;
do the same with the left hand.
Place both hands together at a distance of eight inches from the chest;
slightly bend the middle finger of the right hand.
Move the middle phalanx of the left hand back and forth in the *kun* position.
To move and incite anger.
A mantra common to all the devas: Oṃ ruka karuṇaye svāhā. Written in the eighth month of the fifth year of Bunji.
I collated it against four original editions.
In the third year of the Jia-si cycle of the Xuánzhèng era,
I transcribed it using the Katsurano edition.

Written by Eikō in the fourth year of Kwan’en. Collated against the original manuscript of the Great Monk Yūshō, former Chief Abbot (Daisōjō) and Head Administrator (Hōmu) of the Imperial Temple Shinjōin, in the fourth year of Meiwa, Year of the Pig.
The *Chōchō* (Tidal Waves) of Chikakuin was transcribed from the aforementioned manuscript in the fifth year of Kōan (1793), the Year of the Ox.

In the winter of the second year of Kyōwa (1802), the Year of the Dog, Shuyō of Fukushōmitsu-ji in Northern Kyoto collated this manuscript against the original and had it carved into woodblocks for circulation throughout the world.
Completed by comparing and adding annotations against the original manuscript using the transmitted copy.
Written by Cishun at age forty-three, in his thirty-seventh year since receiving the precepts.
